key_insight: A rubric-based evaluation found that frontier LLMs handled low-stakes rubric items much better than critical clinical reasoning items, revealing a strong mismatch between surface completeness and true clinical priority.
clinical_relevance: For AI-assisted clinical workflows, the results suggest that even top models may miss essential safety-critical reasoning steps, so expert rubrics and high-weight checks are important before any real-world use.
method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios were created across four specialties, each with a weighted atomic rubric derived from a golden answer.
Three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) were scored on 184 total criteria using expert met/not-met labels.
Three LLM autoraters were also tested against expert grading to assess rubric-label agreement.
evidence_signal: Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 for Claude, 0.39 for GPT, and 0.37 for Gemini; critical weight-5 criteria passed only 32.4-41.7%, and 56 of 108 critical criteria were missed by all models.
watch_item: This is a small, preliminary benchmark with only five cases, so the findings are useful for evaluation design but should not be overgeneralized to all clinical settings.
paper_title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
